title: The Callers Who Met a Scholarship Student
text:
Adam Grant, then a doctoral student, studied a university call center where paid fundraisers phoned alumni to ask for donations. The job was repetitive and full of rejection, and turnover was high. Much of the money raised went to scholarships, but the callers rarely saw the students they were helping.

In one field experiment, Grant and his colleagues arranged for one group of callers to meet a student whose scholarship had been funded by the call center. The student spent about five to ten minutes telling them how the money had changed his life and thanking them. A second group read a letter from a student, and a control group had no contact at all.

A month later, the callers who had met the student in person were spending more than twice as much time on the phone each week as before, and they were bringing in more than twice as much money. The callers in the other groups showed no such change. A few minutes face to face with someone who benefited from their work had made the effort feel worthwhile.
lesson: People work harder when they see the person their work helps. Find ways to connect your team with the real people at the other end.
people: Adam Grant, Elizabeth Campbell, Grace Chen, Keenan Cottone, David Lapedis, Karen Lee
location: A public university in the USA
source: Grant, A. M., Campbell, E. M., Chen, G., Cottone, K., Lapedis, D., and Lee, K. (2007). Impact and the art of motivation maintenance: The effects of contact with beneficiaries on persistence behavior. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 103(1), 53-67.
